By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Production

Afrikaaps Fry Notes

Prof Adam Haupt and Chester Williams

Interview. Academic
Visuals at computer
Phone ringing. Submissions on computer.
(What does he speak at home?)
How Afrikaaps was creolised language and then purified and adjusted to Dutch Afrikaans.
Seen by many as colonialization of Afrikaans.
Afrikaans is a mixing pot of languages reflecting the nationalities of those who were brought to the Cape at that time.

Support for the dictionary has exceeded expectations, says professor Quentin Williams, director of the Centre for Multilingualism & Diversities Research at the University of the Western Cape (UWC).

“When we invited submissions, our phones lit up like a Christmas tree.”
Day one of the trilingual dictionary project was July 28. By Friday, the team had about 150,000 words for possible inclusion.
“We started by compiling words from texts written in the language and idiomatic expressions used by authors, and moved on to words from performers, poets, pastors and other sources. They are diverse and quite different to those of the Woordeboek van die Afrikaanse Taal,” says Williams.
The UWC centre and the NGO Heal the Hood are driving the project with support from the University of Cape Town’s Centre for Film & Media Studies.
UCT centre director, professor Adam Haupt, says that excitement about the dictionary spread like wildfire.
Dictionary is in launch form. NO HARD COPY

We’re in the process of training the core editorial board in the scientific area of lexicography, translation and transcription. This includes the archiving of the initial, structured corpus for the dictionary. We will write down definitions and determine meanings of old and new Kaaps words. This process will be subjected to a rigorous review and editing and stylistic process of the Kaaps words we will enter in the dictionary. The entries will include their history of origin, use and uptake. There will also be a translation from standard Afrikaans and English.

Who will use the dictionary?
It will be a resource for its speakers and valuable to educators, students and researchers. It will impact the ways in which institutions, as loci of power, engage speakers of Kaaps. It would also be useful to journalists, publishers and editors keen to learn more about how to engage Kaaps speakers.
A Kaaps dictionary will validate it as a language in its own right. And it will validate the identities of the people who speak it. It will also assist in making visible the diverse cultural, linguistic, geographical and historical tributaries that contributed to the evolution of this language.
HISTORICAL CAPE FOOTAGE – SLAVE MUSEUM
Interview there with one of the curators.

What is Kaaps and who uses the language?
Kaaps or Afrikaaps is a language created in settler colonial South Africa, developed by the 1500s. It took shape as a language during encounters between indigenous African (Khoi and San), South-East Asian, Dutch, Portuguese and English people. It could be argued that Kaaps predates the emergence of an early form of Kaaps-Hollands (the South African variety of Dutch that would help shape Afrikaans). Traders and sailors would have passed through this region well before formal colonisation commenced. Also consider migration and movement on the African continent itself. Every intercultural engagement would have created an opportunity for linguistic exchange and the negotiation of new meaning.

BAKARAT – Interview Amy Jeptha Director – grew up in Cape Flats

MNET Movie – Kaye Anne Williams will have contacts and we can get permission from her.

Film will have lived experiences portrayed in an authentic way. Created a movie show people as multi-dimensional not always living in dire straights.

The first ever film in Afrikaaps - a dialect of Afrikaans, with words from other languages as well - is making waves in South Africa, trying to change the often one-dimensional, negative perception of Cape Town's mixed-race community.
Barakat, which means blessings in Arabic, was filmed in the Cape Flats - a vast low-lying area to the south-east of Cape Town's city centre, where many disenfranchised people were forcibly moved by the former apartheid government in the 1950s.

AMY bio at 33, she’s soaring. Having had her work performed on international stages including New York’s Carnegie Hall, she was 2019’s Standard Bank Young Artist Award recipient for theatre. Her adapted-from-reality screenplay for Ellen: The Ellen Pakkies Story, about a Cape Flats mother who killed her drug-addicted son, not only drew critical acclaim, but had women audience members thanking her, saying, “Your film made me feel like I’ve finally been seen”.
HISTORY OF CAPE FLATS – Created in 1950s by Apartheid gov and current association of association gang lands and drugs. Stock Footage

Heal the Hood co-ordinator Shaquile Southgate says the first formalised dictionary of Kaaps “will instil pride in the language”, one of the first features of identity.
The NGO focuses on youth development on the Cape Flats through the hip-hop culture.
Other options David Kramer – not sure this is PC?
Kaapse Klopse footage
Education – kids have to learn a foreign Afrikaans in their classrooms.

AFRIKAAPS: Script no 9

Up Sound “What else? I don’t know what do you want Mummy to read? Open.”

V/O
It’s story-hour in Mitchell's Plain, Cape Town. Janine Van Rooy-Overmeyer is treating her daughter Adaya Krotoa to poems in her rich mother tongue from a collection of her own writing.

Poem
“One of my children does not know who their father is. He is still so angry, I dare not ask. Because I am also looking for replacements and answers for the father that I don’t know. I don’t want to talk!

I dream that one day I will succeed, the man of my dreams will stay by my side. I had this dream far too long, yet it left me again and again. Maybe this time I can stand on my own.”

V/O
Famous as Blaq Pearl, the gifted author and songwriter joined a group of hip hop artists and activists for Cape Vernacular Afrikaans in staging a musical in 2010. They staked a claim, calling it Afrikaaps…and set in motion a movement to demand recognition and dignity for the brand of Afrikaans widely spoken in the Western Cape.

Blaq Pearl
“Don’t let anyone tell you that the way you speak is incorrect or not good enough, and that is the way we were raised to believe that the way I speak Afrikaans is not good enough and the impact that this has on you that speaks a different kind of Afrikaans that is not what they call standardised makes you feel like you are less you know.”

V/O
It caught on quickly - and now, the expressive dialect birthed on the Cape Flats is forever Afrikaaps, from its root “Afrikaans”...and “die Kaap”...it’s home. But there’s a delicious double meaning in there.

Mac
“Ok you coined the phrase Afrikaaps?”

Jits
Yes

Mac
“Where does it come from?
What does it mean to you?”

Jits
“To kaap something means to hijack.”

Mac
“Ya, kaaping my lyrics”

“Yes taking back history now we belong as much as there is a history of Afrikaans now we actually taking old language and putting ourselves in there and putting ourselves back there. The language itself.”

V/O
It’s a language and a movement. Linguist-activists like hip hop artist Quintin Goliath aka JitsVinger are unshackling the language one richly descriptive word at a time - and with it, an entire people…

Jits
“Why is Afrikaaps so important. Hmm to me because its so beautiful and the people who speak so vibrant. For the longest time we haven’t told our story.”

Link
Afrikaaps is taking centre stage in a new trilingusal dictionary with English, Afrikaans and Afrikaaps, a language long verlooked as marginal but very intrinsic to the Cape culture and now it is getting all the recognition it deserves.

Adam
My favourite word is koesister because I look forward to it every Sunday, the proper way of speaking this language is koeksister but the actualy people say koeisister.

Mac
And then Hallihah – Hawaaian for hello

Marc
Ok, This is our version for oh my word or oh my gosh.

Mac
Awe is hello

Jits
Awe is like someone agreeing with you, awe is like saying korek is this going to be a dope interview, is everybody going to watch this.AWE

FLORIS PLEASE BLEEP FOK

Janine
My favourite word is Awe, befok, kwaai, kwaai means great amazing cool.

V/O
University of Cape Town’s film and media studies expert Prof Adam Haupt says it was the hip hop movement that thrust Afrikaaps into the limelight.

Adam
“In order to understand what hip hop voices where doing was validating black voices in this case, what prophets of the city and in the nineties would call ghoemtaal, was scholars now call kaaps what they were doing was to validate the languages that people in working classes was speaking and so not to feel shame and apologise for my Kombuis afrikaans, and of course that references the history of slavery.

V/O
Kaaps preceded the standardised form of Afrikaans, originating as a non-white creole language under early colonialism - the tongue of slaves and workers. Its roots are Malay, Indonesian, Portuguese and the indigenous San and Khoekhoe.

Eina - for one - a KhoeKhoe word.

And an apt one to describe the apartheid government’s forced removal of disenfranchised coloured workers to the Cape Flats. But Afrikaaps flourished.

Najumoeniesa Damon teaches visitors to the Iziko Slave Lodge this social history.
(We might add Iziko Museums original slave lodge?)

Najumoeniesa
“So even in the slave lodge we had this version of Afrikaans which was spoken which was a broken mixture of Dutch and all the various dialects and language that were introduced by the slaves that were forced to live within this space.”

Link
The Auwal Mosque here in the Bokaap in CT is recognised as the forst mosque established in the country Afrikaans was first taught here in Madaris or Islamic schools and the language was written in Arabic.

Najumoeniesa
When they read it back they read it in the pidgeon Dutch and it was written in the Arabic script.

Blaq Pearl
We went to UCT and we found out that the first Afrikaans had been written in Arabic and I was like HUH, what is this why is this information not taught at school.

V/O
Afrikaans became an official language from 1925 and progressively a tool of racial oppression Standardised through translations of the Bible and dictionaries - not even those who loved Afrikaans could save it from it’s darkest hours under apartheid.

Najumoeniesa

“They decided that their version be the official version that will be acceptable and all the other dialects wouldn’t be acceptable and Afrikaaps was one of those dialect that wasn’t acceptable. Even though it was one of the groups that was spoken most in Cape Town.”

“Afrikaans is not slang, Afrikaaps is not broken, Afrikaaps is not a leser version of anything spoken, its rich in history, it’s diverse in structure, it’s the linguistic identity of an entire culture.”

V/O
An ARGITEKBEK is a poet - directly translated: a mouth-architect. Blaq Pearl and JitsVinger are two of those who contributed words for the Afrikaaps dictionary.

Blaq Pearl
And I felt so proud, immediately I made the change physically whenever I go into those spaces ek sal praat the way ek praat niemand gaan vir my niks se nie. Niemand gaan vir my laat junk voel nie. Ek gaan net praat soos ek praat, take me or leave me dit is soos dit is.




VO
Afrikaaps now even has its own rags - Marc Lottering co-founded a clothing brand that trades on and promotes the best of Afrikaaps expressions.

Marc
“So they can see oh I can actually say this in public and this has been on ads or been on social media and the more and more people start to use it the more acceptable it becomes and people know it is nt gang related and not negative, it’s just an expression of who we are.

Link
What the dictionary has given is a way for people to be their authentic selves and as the well known brand Vanniekaap says, they say you mustn’t dream you must just dala.

V/O
I asked Jits for a couple of pointers while walking the streets of Cape Town.

Jits
The most obvious one is Bru watter size dra jy. He’s gonna take your shoes.

Laughs
Your shoes are gone Size 9 Bru laughs

V/O
Professor Adam Haupt and the team have collated around 100 000 words to date and they say it will take at least three years for the Afrikaaps dictionary to get into print.

Adam
And so that is the point of this mission is to allow teachers to be able to access the resource a dictionary here is a resource by leading scholars, you may use this, so when a kid in your classrooms speak in a particular way you can point to it and use it as your guide. And you can bring people together.

Marc
With everything that is being done right now it is to bring Afrikaaps to the same level as Afrikaans and maybe the two join together and move into the sunset – who knows?

Jits
Lekke my broer my man, Lekke

Promo 1 or Tuesday Teaser

Mac
Awe Ouens
A new trilingual dictionary with English, Afrikaans and Afrikaaps has brought dignity to a language that has always been seen as slang or associated with gangsterism.

Jits
Awe is like someone agreeing with you, awe is like saying korek is this going to be a dope interview, is everybody going to watch this. AWE

Promo 2

Adam
My actual favourite word is Koesister.

Awe is like when you are agreeing with something

Haalihah is oh my word or Oh my gosh

Kwaai means great amazing cool

V/O
And isn’t it kwaai that there is a new trilingual dictionary in English Afrikaans and Afrikaaps

Link
A language long overlooked as marginal but very intrinsic to the Cape Culture.

Promo

V/O
Afrikaans was first written in Arabic Script here at the Auwal Mosque in
Cape Town in the 18th Century.

Najumoeniesa
“When they read it back they read it back in the pigeon Afrikaans/pidgeon Dutch.

V/O
It was a creole language made up from all the nationalities in the Cape. But what happened to the Kaaps Hollands dialect, that is now taking centre stage as Afrikaaps.





Promo
Mac
“Ok you coined the phrase Afrikaaps?”

Jits
“Yes”

Mac
“Where does it come from?”

Jits
“To Kaap something means to hijack.
So, for me it was taking the history back now.”

V/o
JitsVinger and other cultural activists have taken
Cape Vernacular Afrikaans or Afrikaaps and put it on the linguistic map.
Giving it the dignity it deserves.
